concept_html:
Access control decides who opens an item. Sensitivity labels say how sensitive its content is, and travel with it. Fabric uses labels from Microsoft Purview Information Protection. You need a Purview licence, and labelling Power BI items also needs a Pro or Premium Per User licence (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026).

How labels spread:

  • Downstream inheritance. A label on a semantic model flows to the reports and dashboards built on it. It never overwrites a label someone applied manually, and never replaces a label with a less restrictive one.
  • Default and mandatory labelling. Admins can apply a default label to new items, or require users to pick one before they save.
  • Export. Labels, and the protection a Purview policy attaches, stay with data exported to Excel, PDF and PowerPoint.

Protection policies link a label to access. When an item carries the label, users and groups named in the policy keep the permissions they already have. Everyone else is blocked. The user who last applied the label is not blocked.

Purview also gives you:

  • Unified Catalog: metadata about Fabric items, visible in Purview.
  • Data loss prevention (DLP): detects sensitive data uploaded to OneLake and raises policy tips and alerts. It also restricts access to sensitive assets in KQL databases, SQL databases and warehouses.
  • Audit: compliance admins track label activity.

Lineage shows how items connect. Every workspace has a lineage view that any user with a workspace role can open. It covers all items in the workspace, plus external sources one step upstream. Impact analysis starts from one item and lists the downstream items and workspaces a change might affect, and lets you notify their contacts.

Run impact analysis before a schema change. A label names the risk. A protection policy acts on it.

exercises.prompt: Write `inherit_label(current: str | None, manual: bool, upstream: str, order: list[str]) -> str | None`. It returns the downstream item's label after its upstream item's label becomes `upstream`. `order` lists labels from least to most restrictive. Rules: a manual label is kept. An unlabelled item takes `upstream`. Otherwise the item takes `upstream` only if it is more restrictive than `current`. Raise `ValueError` if a label is not in `order`.
exercises.prompt_html: Write inherit_label(current: str | None, manual: bool, upstream: str, order: list[str]) -> str | None. It returns the downstream item's label after its upstream item's label becomes upstream. order lists labels from least to most restrictive. Rules: a manual label is kept. An unlabelled item takes upstream. Otherwise the item takes upstream only if it is more restrictive than current. Raise ValueError if a label is not in order.
exercises.solution:
def inherit_label(
    current: str | None, manual: bool, upstream: str, order: list[str]
) -> str | None:
    """Downstream label after the upstream label changes.

    Args:
        current: The downstream item's label, or None.
        manual: Whether a person applied the current label.
        upstream: The upstream item's new label.
        order: Labels from least to most restrictive.

    Returns:
        The downstream item's label after inheritance.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a label is not in order.
    """
    for label in (current, upstream):
        if label is not None and label not in order:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown label: {label}")
    if current is None:
        return upstream
    if manual:
        return current
    if order.index(upstream) > order.index(current):
        return upstream
    return current

title: Sensitivity labels, Purview and lineage
why_html: An engineer renamed a column in a lakehouse table on a Friday. Monday morning, 14 reports in three other workspaces showed errors, and a finance close was delayed. Impact analysis on the table would have listed all 14 reports and their workspaces, and notified their owners before the change.
